clinicalPearls: Type 2 (idiopathic perifoveal) is by far the most common form, presenting in middle age with gradual bilateral blurring, metamorphopsia and difficulty reading despite a relatively preserved distance acuity early on.

The perifoveal telangiectatic vessels are frequently subtle on ophthalmoscopy; the diagnosis often rests on characteristic optical coherence tomography and fluorescein angiographic findings rather than the visible fundus appearance.
A loss of retinal transparency with a greyish sheen temporal to the fovea, right-angled venules and refractile crystalline deposits at the inner retinal surface are classic type 2 signs.
Optical coherence tomography shows hyporeflective inner and outer retinal cavities and, importantly, disruption of the ellipsoid zone without correspondingly large fluid accumulation.
Depletion of the parafoveal Muller cells and macular pigment is a central feature, and macular pigment optical density imaging can reveal a characteristic parafoveal loss.

Fluorescein angiography demonstrates deep telangiectatic capillaries that leak in the late phase, typically temporal to the fovea, but this leakage does not respond to the anti-angiogenic or laser strategies used for other exudative maculopathies.
Type 2 is subdivided into a non-proliferative stage and a sight-threatening proliferative stage in which subretinal neovascularisation grows from the deep retinal circulation.
Type 1 (aneurysmal telangiectasia) is usually unilateral, males predominate, and it behaves more like a congenital retinal vascular anomaly with exudation akin to Coats disease.
reference.pathophysiology: Macular telangiectasia type 2 is now understood primarily as a neurodegenerative disorder of the macula in which the Muller glial cells, which maintain retinal architecture and the blood-retinal barrier and sequester macular pigment, are progressively depleted in the parafoveal region. Loss of these glial cells produces retinal cavitation, photoreceptor (ellipsoid zone) disruption and secondary abnormalities of the deep retinal capillary network that manifest as the visible telangiectasia; the vascular changes are therefore considered a consequence rather than the primary event. Impaired retinal handling of serine and glycine metabolism has been implicated, and reduced circulating serine with accumulation of neurotoxic deoxysphingolipids is associated with the condition. In the proliferative stage, ischaemia and glial loss permit neovascular complexes to invade from the deep capillary plexus into the subretinal space, causing haemorrhage, exudation and disciform scarring. Type 1 disease, by contrast, reflects a developmental telangiectatic and aneurysmal malformation of the retinal capillaries with breakdown of the inner blood-retinal barrier and lipid exudation.
additionalDifferentials: Branch retinal vein occlusion with macular telangiectasia
Coats disease and other exudative retinal telangiectasias
Macular hole or pseudohole causing metamorphopsia
additionalInvestigations: Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography for retinal cavitation and ellipsoid zone integrity
Fluorescein angiography demonstrating deep temporal parafoveal telangiectasia and late leakage
Optical coherence tomography angiography to map deep capillary plexus abnormalities and detect neovascularisation
Fundus autofluorescence showing loss of the normal foveal masking by macular pigment
Blue-light or confocal imaging of refractile crystalline deposits
redFlags: New or worsening metamorphopsia with subretinal fluid suggesting progression to the proliferative neovascular stage
Sudden central visual loss from subretinal haemorrhage
Development of a full-thickness macular hole
Rapidly enlarging pigment plaque or disciform scar involving fixation
Marked exudation or a retinal detachment in suspected type 1 (aneurysmal) disease
reference.prognosis: Non-proliferative type 2 typically causes slow, progressive parafoveal visual decline over years with relatively preserved distance acuity until late, whereas the proliferative stage can cause rapid central loss from neovascular haemorrhage and scarring. Anti-angiogenic therapy is reserved for the proliferative neovascular stage and does not benefit the non-proliferative leakage; overall central vision often remains functional for reading tasks for a prolonged period.
pitfalls: Mistaking the subtle telangiectasia and leakage for diabetic maculopathy and applying focal laser or anti-angiogenic injections that are ineffective in non-proliferative disease.
Interpreting late fluorescein leakage as an indication for treatment when it does not correlate with treatable exudation in type 2.
Overlooking the diagnosis when distance acuity is preserved and the fundus appears near-normal, delaying recognition of the ellipsoid zone loss on optical coherence tomography.
Failing to distinguish the neurodegenerative type 2 from the vascular malformation type 1, which have different natural histories and management.
Attributing reading difficulty and metamorphopsia to early cataract or refractive error rather than examining the macula in detail.
